column1: # Navier–Stokes full-script03 extraction. Frederick Surrey. Evidence-bound production draft.

column2: This wind tunnel exists only inside a computer.
Air enters on the left, flows past a cylinder, and leaves on the right. We release dye at the inlet, so we can see where the air goes.
Behind the cylinder, the dye will make shapes, and some may curl into swirls. This film is about one question. Which of those swirls belong to the air, and which did our computer invent, or erase?
A computer can't follow every bit of air. It cuts the tunnel into small cells, and keeps a few numbers for each one.

So here's a test we'll come back to. Pick one thing to measure downstream, such as how often the flow there swings from side to side, if it swings at all. Then make every cell half as wide and half as tall, which takes four times as many cells, and measure again.

If the answer changes a lot, the cells are still shaping it, and we haven't yet shown what the air itself does. So first we'll build the core of the program by hand. What it stores, the law it follows, and the one step where every cell has to agree with its neighbors at once. Pressure.
Before you trust any picture of a flow, ask what it's a picture of.
What the program computes is the velocity, which way the air moves and how fast, all through the tunnel. Drawn as arrows, it's a snapshot of one instant.
Dye is different. The air carries it along, and it doesn't push back. It also remembers. The dye you see now carries a record of the past.
Here's a flow we can work out exactly. A nozzle releases dye steadily for eight seconds.
The dye has closed into a loop, eight meters around. Is the air swirling?

No. At every instant, all the air moves the same way, at one meter per second, so nothing spins and there's no center it all turns around. Only the direction turns, once around every eight seconds. The loop is a record of that turning.
So one flow gives three different curves. A streamline follows the arrows at one instant. Here, the streamlines are straight lines.

A pathline is the track of one bit of air over time. The first puff from the nozzle went around a circle above it, and it has just arrived back. Every bit of air makes the same loop, each around its own center.
And a streakline is everything that passed through one point, wherever it is now. That's what continuous dye shows. Here, it's the circle below the nozzle.
Three curves, one flow. When the flow doesn't change in time, all three are the same curve. When it does change, they can come apart, as they did here.

Dye from a nozzle is always a streakline. In our tunnel, the flow behind the cylinder may change in time, and then that streakline can differ from the streamlines. So a curl in the dye is not proof of a swirl in the air.
To see what the air is doing at one instant, we'll draw arrows and streamlines from the same saved moment of the same run. And we'll always say which view we're showing.
Dye is for us. What the program has to get right is the velocity. So what makes velocity change?
Take one small bit of air, a parcel, and follow it.
Here's a simpler flow we can write down exactly. Air moves through a channel that narrows from four meters wide to two, over a length of two meters.

This flow never changes. Stand at any point, and the arrow there stays the same forever. Down the middle, the speed is two meters per second at the entrance, three halfway along, and four at the exit.
Release a parcel at the entrance, on the center line. It's moving at two meters per second, and for every meter it travels, the flow around it gets one meter per second faster.
Nothing changes at any fixed point. So how fast is the parcel speeding up as it enters? Zero, one, or two meters per second, every second?

Two. In a tiny moment, it moves a tiny distance at two meters per second, and each meter of that distance adds one meter per second of speed. Two times one. Its speed rises at two meters per second, every second.
At the exit it's moving at four, through the same climb, so there it's speeding up at four. It crosses the whole channel in about seven tenths of a second.

So there are two different questions. Standing still, how fast does the velocity change at this spot? Here, not at all. Riding along, how fast does your velocity change? That's the one Newton's law needs, because forces act on the parcel, not on a spot.

Riding along, the change has two parts. The flow might be changing where you are. And you're moving to where the flow is different, which counts as your speed, times how fast the flow changes along your way.
Together, they make the material derivative. It's the change you'd feel riding with the fluid.

That second part is called advection. It is not a force. Something is pushing this parcel faster, and we'll find it next. Advection is the bookkeeping that connects what we see at fixed points to what each parcel feels.
In our tunnel, the gap beside the cylinder narrows too. Air passing through it changes speed, even if the flow there never changes at all.
Newton's law says force equals mass times acceleration. For a parcel of fluid, the forces come from three places.
First, pressure. The air around the parcel presses on every side. Equal pressure all around adds up to nothing. What pushes is a difference, more pressure behind than in front.

So the push points from high pressure toward low, and its strength is how fast the pressure falls along the way. That's minus the pressure gradient. Divide by the density, and you have the acceleration it causes.
In our channel, the parcel at the entrance speeds up at two meters per second, every second. So the pressure must fall ahead of it, steeply enough to push each kilogram with two newtons.
Air is light. For this example, we'll take its density to be one point three kilograms per cubic meter. Then that push needs a pressure drop of just two point six pascals for each meter.
Second, viscosity. Neighboring layers of fluid drag on each other. A faster layer pulls a slower neighbor forward, and the slower one holds it back.
Here are three layers moving at one, two and three meters per second. Is the middle layer pulled forward, held back, or neither?

Neither. Both pulls are real, and the fast layer pulls it forward exactly as hard as the slow layer holds it back. When the speed climbs evenly from layer to layer, viscosity's net pull is zero. Only a bend leaves a net pull.

Make the speeds one, three and three. Now the middle layer is faster than the average of its neighbors, which is two, so it's held back. Viscosity pulls each bit of fluid toward the average of what's around it.
In symbols, that's nu times the Laplacian of the velocity. Nu, the kinematic viscosity, says how quickly that drag evens out the speeds.
In our channel, each part of the velocity changes in a straight line from place to place, with no bend. So viscosity's pulls cancel there too, and its net pull is zero. It's all pressure.

Third, forces that act on the whole parcel at once, like gravity. We write f for the force on each kilogram. In our tunnel, gravity's only effect is a pressure that rises steadily with depth. So we fold it into the pressure, and set f to zero. But f belongs in the law.
Add the three, and you have the parcel's acceleration. Minus the pressure gradient over density, plus nu times the Laplacian of velocity, plus f.
Each term is a force on one kilogram, which is the same thing as meters per second, every second.
We still haven't said what sets the pressure. The answer is a rule about volume.
Air can be squeezed. But we'll keep the air in our tunnel far slower than sound, where its density barely changes, and treat it as incompressible. Every parcel keeps its volume.

Here's what that means for one square of the channel, one meter on a side. Air comes in through its left side at two meters per second. It leaves through the right at three. And through the top, it comes in at one.
In, two plus one. Out, three. Nothing piles up, and nothing drains.
Net outflow from a small region, divided by its size, is called the divergence. Incompressible means the divergence is zero, everywhere, at every moment.

Notice what didn't happen. The speeds aren't all equal. Air leaves this square faster than it entered from the left, because more arrives through the top. Constant density doesn't mean constant speed.

Now the tunnel. Draw two slices across it, from wall to wall. The walls and the cylinder let nothing through. So whatever flows in through one slice must flow out through the other, at the same moment.
Suppose the cylinder blocks a quarter of the tunnel's height.
Compared with the inlet, how fast must the air move, on average, through the open part of that slice?
Four thirds as fast. The same flow has to fit through three quarters of the height.
That's a rule the program must keep in every cell, at every step. Keeping it is pressure's job.
We now have every piece, so we can write the law.
On the left, a parcel's acceleration. It's the change at a fixed point, plus advection, the change from moving.
On the right, the forces on each kilogram. Minus the pressure gradient over density, viscosity's pull toward the average, and any outside force, f.
And underneath, the rule that nothing piles up. The divergence of the velocity is zero.
These are the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, for a fluid of constant density and viscosity.
In our flat tunnel, they're three equations for three unknowns at every point. Two parts of the velocity, and the pressure.
But look at pressure. The velocity has an equation that says how it changes in time. Pressure has none. It's whatever it needs to be to keep the divergence zero.
Check the units. Every term is meters per second, per second.
Equations alone aren't a problem we can solve. We also need where the flow starts, and what happens at its edges.

At the start, we say what the velocity is everywhere. At the inlet, we choose how the air comes in. At the walls and the cylinder, air can't pass through. And because it's viscous, it doesn't slide either. Right at a surface, it moves with the surface.
At the outlet, we need a rule that lets air leave, and that rule is our choice, not nature's. Change any of these, and you have a different problem, with a different answer.
So far this is mathematics. Now we have to turn it into something a computer can store.
A computer can't store a velocity at every point. There are too many points. So we cut the tunnel into cells, and keep a few numbers for each.
Where we keep those numbers matters. We'll put each cell's pressure at its center. And we'll keep velocity on the faces between cells, only the part that crosses each face.
This is called a staggered grid, or a MAC grid.
It makes the volume rule easy to check. A cell's net outflow is just its four faces. For our square from the channel, three out on the right, two in on the left, one in at the top. Zero.
And every inside face is shared by two cells. What leaves one enters the other. Add up every cell's balance, and each inside face cancels itself out. Only the edges of the tunnel are left.

Let's shrink this to something we can do by hand. Imagine dividing this box of fluid into four squares. These lines are imaginary. We will call each one a face. Fluid can cross them. The outside walls are solid, so nothing crosses the edge of the box.
Whatever happens inside, what must the four cells' imbalances add up to?
Zero. Each inside face adds to one cell and takes away from another, and the walls carry nothing. That's true for any flow at all in a sealed box.
Here's how the program moves time forward, one small step at a time.
First it makes a provisional velocity. It carries the velocity along with the flow, lets viscosity smooth it, and adds any outside forces. Call the result u-star.
Those first steps ignored the volume rule. So u-star usually leaves some cells gaining fluid, and others losing it.

The last step fixes that. It measures each cell's imbalance, and finds a pressure whose push cancels it. That push runs from high pressure toward low, and we add it to u-star. Then every cell balances, and the step is done.

Suppose our provisional calculation sends fluid from A to B at speed one, with no movement across the other three internal faces. A would lose fluid while B gained it. That provisional answer does not satisfy incompressibility. We need to correct it before accepting the step.
Pressure will change these velocities. After the correction, how much of that original speed remains across the face between A and B? All of it, none, or something in between?

One quarter remains. The other faces start moving too. The corrected flow goes from A to B, B to D, D to C and C back to A, at a quarter on each face. Every square now has exactly as much coming in as going out.
Fixing the flow on one face moved all four. Next, how the pressure step found that answer, and why each cell's answer depends on its neighbors'.

Here is how the pressure calculation finds that answer. The pressure difference between neighboring cells changes the velocity on their shared face. The correction pushes from higher pressure toward lower pressure. So the equation for one cell contains its own pressure and its neighbors' pressures.
Do that for every cell, and you get four linked equations.
Each corner cell has a two on the diagonal, because it has two neighbors that fluid can cross to. Deep inside a bigger grid, a cell would have four.

These equations are linked. Changing the pressure in one cell changes the corrections on its shared faces, which changes the balances its neighbors need. We must solve a coupled problem, even if our numerical method improves the answer through many local updates.

B has the highest pressure, where the provisional flow would pile fluid up. A has the lowest, where it would drain. B pushes back into A and up into D. C pushes down into A. And D pushes left into C. These are corrections to the first guess, not the final flow by themselves.
Only differences matter. Add the same constant to every pressure and none of the face corrections changes. We can choose a reference pressure to make the answer unique.

Add up the flow around the loop, counting each face in the direction of travel. Before the correction, that total is one, all on the face from A to B. Now follow the pressure differences around the same loop. Every pressure appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so they cancel. The correction cannot change the flow's loop total, so it stays one. In this tiny box, the only balanced pattern is a loop with the same speed on every face. Four faces share one, so each carries a quarter. That is also why the answer could not be zero.
If we stop the pressure solve early, the leftover isn't hidden. Whatever the equations miss by in each cell shows up as exactly that much imbalance in the cell, with the sign flipped.

Written for smooth fields, the same step reads like this. The Laplacian of pressure equals the density over the time step, times the divergence of u-star. Then the new velocity is u-star, minus the time step over the density, times the pressure gradient.
This pressure is the one that makes this step's velocity balance. It isn't the air's absolute pressure, the kind a barometer reads. Only its differences ever enter.

And the formula isn't the whole method. The divergence and the gradient must be built from the same faces and cells, or the correction can miss the imbalance it measured. The walls, inlet and outlet shape the matrix too, the way the box's walls turned four into two.

Our tunnel has the same structure, with far more cells. Every step ends with a pressure puzzle that links all of them. How quickly we can solve it, and how closely, is part of what decides how far we can trust the picture. That's where we go next.

Every time step ends in this last card, with a pressure puzzle to solve. The four-cell box we could solve all at once. With many more cells, a program can instead start from a guess and improve it with many small, local fixes.
To see how that works, we'll use a simpler shape, eight cells in a row, like a narrow pipe. The left end is a solid wall. The right end opens into a big tank, where the pressure is held at zero.

Now let's rig a test where we already know the answer. Suppose the provisional flow already balances in every cell. Then the right pressure correction is zero everywhere. But our program starts from an old guess, so all of that guess is error.

This guess is wrong in two different ways. There's a broad hump, highest at the wall and sinking toward the tank. And on top of it there's a zigzag, every other cell half a unit too high, and the cells between half a unit too low.

Here's a simple local fix, one a cell can make by itself. Look at its neighbors' pressures, and move halfway toward their average. The tank counts as a neighbor at zero, and the wall doesn't count at all. When every cell does this at once, that's one sweep.
In solver language, this is called smoothing. But it smooths the mistake in our guess, not the air. It's a different thing from the viscosity on the second card.
Try it on the zigzag alone. What does one sweep do to it? Flip it, halve it, or erase it?

It erases it. Each cell's neighbors sit on the other side, so their average is the opposite value, and halfway lands exactly on zero. Only the last cell keeps a little, an eighth, because one of its neighbors is the tank.

Why only halfway? If every cell jumped all the way to its neighbors' average, the zigzag would just flip. High cells would become low and low cells high, and the next sweep would flip most of them back.
Now the broad hump. Each cell's neighbors average to almost exactly its own value, so halfway is hardly a move at all. The first sweep barely shifts the middle cells, while the error is nearly one.

What the equations miss by in each cell, the leftover imbalance from chapter nine, is called the residual. For this hump, no cell's residual is above three hundredths, though the pressure is off by nearly one. Each cell's move is set by its residual, so small residuals mean small moves.

Now run sweeps on the whole guess and watch. The first sweep wipes out the zigzag, except for that eighth beside the tank, and the error drops from about one and a half to just under one. After that the error barely moves. Twenty sweeps later, it's still above eight tenths.

Fast at first, then stuck. A classic paper on these methods describes exactly that. A local fix only sees its neighbors, so it's quick with mistakes about the size of a cell, and slow with broad ones.

And finer grids make it worse. Along this tube, halving the broad error took seventy-three sweeps with eight cells, two hundred ninety-six with sixteen, and about twelve hundred with thirty-two. Each doubling meant about four times as many sweeps.
That's bad news for our question card. To test whether halving the cells changes the answer, we need finer grids, and that's exactly where these sweeps slow down most.
Here's the turn. After a few sweeps, what's left of the error is broad. And a broad shape doesn't need small cells to describe it. So let's describe it on a coarser grid, with cells twice as wide.
But the program can't see the error. It only sees the residuals. Luckily, the error solves the same kind of pressure puzzle, with the residuals on the right side of the equations.
So add up the residuals in each pair. The face between the two halves cancels, just as every inside face cancelled in chapter seven's ledger. That leaves one number for each coarse cell.
On the coarse grid, the same pressure rule holds, with cells twice as wide. There are four cells instead of eight. And this puzzle is small enough to solve exactly.
Then we bring the answer back to the fine cells, by drawing straight lines between the coarse values. That's the correction, and we'll add it to our guess.
Before this correction, the largest error is almost one. How big is it after? About half, about a tenth, or about two hundredths?
About two hundredths. One small four-cell solve removed almost all of the broad error that the sweeps could barely touch.

The correction leaves small kinks, so we finish with two more sweeps. They bring the largest residual from about two hundredths to about four thousandths, and the error to just under two hundredths. Sweeps alone would have needed four hundred eighteen to get the error that low.
A second round, with three sweeps, a coarse correction and two more sweeps, shrinks the error again.
Why sweep first? What if we skip the sweeps and go straight to the coarse grid? Would the error shrink, stay about the same, or grow?

It grows, from about one and a half to over seven. Each coarse cell holds just one number, so it can't see a zigzag. In the middle of the tube, each pair's zigzag residuals cancel. But at the wall and at the tank they don't, and the coarse grid mistakes those leftovers for a broad error.
So in this round, the sweeps come first. They clear the zigzag, and the coarse grid gets only the smooth part, which it can describe.

Now the catch. In this test we know the right answer, so we can see the error. For an unknown answer, the solver cannot directly measure this error. All it measures is the residual, and that's a different number.

Go back to the guess after three sweeps. No cell's residual is above about four hundredths. But the pressure is off by almost one. And the flow, which should be zero everywhere, is off by up to about two tenths.
The small imbalances add up. Each face carries the sum of all the imbalances between it and the wall, so along the tube they pile up into a real flow.

So a solver can use the residual to decide when to stop. Basilisk, a free, open-source fluid code, by default stops once no cell would gain or lose more than a thousandth of its volume in one time step. If a hundred rounds aren't enough, it stops anyway and prints a warning.

Passing that test limits the imbalance, not the error, and after a warning, even the imbalance is still above the limit. So when we judge a picture, we'll ask two separate questions. Did the solver leave only small imbalances? And does tightening its tolerance, or refining the grid, change what we see?

On a big grid, the coarse puzzle is still big. So we treat it the same way, with a few sweeps and then an even coarser grid, down to one so small it's cheap to handle. That ladder of grids is called multigrid.
Each level fixes the mistakes that look small from where it stands. And these coarse grids live only inside the pressure solve. They don't change the grid the flow itself is computed on.
We have seen how different grids can tackle different scales of error. Now, back to carrying the flow along.

Back to the first card of every step, carry. The program moves the velocity, and the dye, along with the flow. It sounds like the easy part. It's also a place where a computer can quietly change the answer.
Here's a test we can check exactly. A straight pipe, a steady wind, and one pulse of dye, four cells wide.

For this test, the dye doesn't spread on its own. So the exact answer is simple. The pulse slides downstream and keeps its shape. We'll ride along with the wind, so the exact pulse stands still on screen.
But the program keeps only one number per cell. Each step, the wind moves the dye half a cell. So the dye in each cell came from halfway between two cells.
The plainest choice is to blend those two cells, half and half. Call it the blend. After one step, the cells at the pulse's edges hold one half.
Now repeat that, step after step, until the dye has ridden twenty-four cells. How tall is the peak now? Still about one, about three quarters, or less than half?
Less than half. The peak is down to about zero point four three, and the dye has spread across many more cells. The exact pulse never changed shape.
And nothing blew up. At every step, every cell stayed between zero and one, and the total stayed at exactly four. The blend is stable, and it's wrong.
This smearing looks like diffusion, as if the dye were spreading out on its own. It's called numerical diffusion. It comes from the method, not from the dye.
So how do we tell it apart from real spreading? With the question we started with. Halve the cells, halve the step along with them, and send the pulse the same distance.
Measure the spreading the way diffusion is measured, by how much the pulse's width squared has grown. On the first cells, the blend added twelve. On cells half as wide, six. Half again, three.
Real spreading wouldn't care what cells or steps we use. This does. Each halving cuts it in half. That change is the method's fingerprint.

Now give the dye a slow spreading of its own, one we choose and declare. The total spreading becomes eighteen, then twelve, then nine. The dye's own share is six every time. Only the method's share shrinks.

On these three rows, the method's share halves each time. If that keeps up, it heads toward zero, and what's left is the spreading we declared. That's what refining is for. But finer rows would also need much smaller steps, for a reason we'll meet in the next chapter.
Velocity has the same two kinds of smoothing. The air's viscosity is in the law, and we declare it. But the carry step smears the velocity too, and that acts like extra viscosity nobody declared.
In the tunnel, that's how a computer can erase a swirl. It rounds off small swirls, the way it rounded off this pulse. That's the first suspect, erased.
Can a sharper rule do better? Instead of blending two cells, fit a smooth curve through four, and read it where the dye came from.
Here's the first step, at the pulse's front edge. Can a cell end up holding less than no dye?

Yes. Just ahead of the pulse, the curve dips to minus one sixteenth, and it dips the same way just behind. Just inside each edge, it overshoots to seventeen sixteenths. The rule has invented dye that can't exist.

After the same twenty-four cells, the curve keeps the peak much better, at about zero point nine. But ripples spread out on both sides, dipping to about minus six hundredths. Our spreading meter reads zero, only because the dips below zero cancel the widening. Once dye goes negative, the meter no longer measures width.
That's the second suspect, invented. A sharper method can draw wiggles that were never in the flow.
A blunter fix is to clamp. Never let the curve's value go below or above the two cells it falls between. Now no cell is ever negative. But watch the total.
After the same trip, the total is down to about three point seven nine. Clamping threw away about a twentieth of the dye. It keeps the values in range. It doesn't keep the amount.
There's a way to keep both. Move the dye the way we balanced cells before, across faces. Whatever leaves one cell enters the next, so the total can't change. Then limit how much crosses each face.
On this pulse, the face rule kept every cell between zero and one at every step, and the total at exactly four. The peak ends at about zero point six two. Sharper than the blend, and still not exact.
Here are all four, after the same trip. The curve has the smallest error, but it invents negative dye. Clamping loses dye. And the blend smears the most.
The face rule sits in between. It keeps every cell in range and every bit of dye. No rule wins every column.
So stable isn't the same as right. Staying in range isn't enough either, and neither is keeping the total. We choose a rule by measuring its error as the cells shrink, not by how good it looks.

One more thing to watch for. Some programs add a force that spins swirls back up, to replace what smearing erased. That's a new model, not part of the law we wrote. If we ever use one, we'll label it.
Cells cut up space. Steps cut up time. The step size is a choice too, and it can change the answer.
Count it in cells per step. So far, the wind moved the dye half a cell each step. What if we take bigger steps?
Here's a second rule, the neighbor rule. Each cell mixes with its upstream neighbor, with weights set by the step. At half a cell per step, it gives exactly the blend, cell for cell.
Now take steps of one and a half cells. The neighbor rule now gives the cell's own dye a weight of minus one half. What happens to the pulse? Does it smear more, smear less, or blow up?
It blows up. After one step, one cell holds one and a half, and another holds minus a half. After ten steps, more than a hundred and fifty, and almost minus a hundred and fifty.
And the total stayed at exactly four the whole time. Keeping the total didn't save it.
Why? Follow one bit of dye. In one step it crosses one and a half cells, but the neighbor rule only looks one cell back. Where the dye came from is out of its reach.

That's the idea behind the C F L condition, named for Courant, Friedrichs and Lewy. As cells and steps shrink together, a method can only home in on the true answer if it reads from everywhere that answer depends on.
For the neighbor rule, that limit is one cell per step, and it's also exactly where this rule stops being stable. Other rules have other limits. So we'll always say which rule a limit belongs to.

The blend doesn't use a fixed neighbor. It looks back to wherever the dye came from, one and a half cells, and blends the two cells there. At this step size, every cell still stays between zero and one.
And here's a surprise. After the same twenty-four cells, the bigger steps left a taller peak, about zero point six seven instead of zero point four three. Fewer steps meant fewer blends.
At exactly one cell per step, the blend is perfect, because each cell just copies its neighbor. And halving the step, to a quarter cell, makes the smearing worse, eighteen instead of twelve.
Don't take that as advice. This wind is the same everywhere, so looking back is exact. In a real flow the speed changes along the way, and the look-back itself has an error that grows with the step.
So stable at any step size is a promise about this rule, in this wind. It isn't a promise about a whole fluid program, and it isn't a promise of accuracy.
To see the step's own error, go back to the narrowing channel. There are no cells this time, only the exact flow. Where is the parcel after half a second?
It's about one point three meters in. A program steps it forward, using the parcel's speed at the start of each step. With steps of an eighth of a second, it ends up about nine centimeters short.
Now halve the step. What happens to the miss? Does it halve, shrink to a quarter, or stay the same?
It about halves, to five centimeters. Each halving of the step roughly halves the miss. That's called a first order method.
A better step uses the speed halfway through each step. Then it's only about four millimeters short. Halve the step, and it's about one millimeter, roughly a quarter. That's second order.

That's the time mesh, with an error of its own. In chapter eleven, we halved the cells and the step together. Now we refine the step with the cells fixed, and then the cells with a fixed step that's small enough for the finest ones.

Viscosity has a step limit of its own. Go back to the layers, now alternating one and three meters per second. Each layer is pulled toward its two neighbors' average, three for a slow layer and one for a fast one. The real stack would settle at two.

A simple step moves each layer by its pull, times the step. Take a big step, and every layer overshoots two. At the limit, each layer lands right on its neighbors' average, so they swap, three and one, forever. Double that step, and they jump to five and minus one.
And that limit tightens fast. Halve the spacing between layers, and the largest safe step shrinks to a quarter. That's why chapter eleven's finer rows would need much smaller steps.
An implicit step solves for all the layers' new speeds together, much as the pressure step solves for all the cells. It stays stable at any step size.

But with the step that blew up before, it leaves a fifth of the zig-zag. Solved exactly in time, these layers keep less than two hundredths. Implicit viscosity removes the step limit. It doesn't remove the error.

So there are three things to refine. The cells, the step, and how closely we solve the pressure puzzle each step. We refine each one on its own, and keep going until no change moves the answer by more than an amount we declared in advance.
Back in our tunnel, that's the test it has to pass. Halve the cells, then halve the step, and see whether the answer moves by more than we allowed.

Our computer now has several ways to be wrong. We can solve the pressure puzzle more carefully and still smear the dye. We can carry the dye more accurately and still step too far through time. There isn't one accuracy knob.
So let's keep a ledger. Beside each result, write what we changed, what we measured, and what that comparison can actually tell us.

First, the unfinished solve. Hold the cells and the time step fixed, and ask the pressure solver to leave a smaller imbalance. Then compare the flow and the quantity we care about. A smaller residual is useful evidence. It isn't the whole answer.

Next, the time step. Keep the grid fixed and take smaller steps. Also refine cells and step together. Keep the same cells traveled per step where stability permits. An explicit diffusion step can require time steps to shrink faster, with the square of cell width. Compare the valid routes: for some rules, changing the step changes the grid error too. Record both sizes and the stability limits.

Our dye pulse shows how the step can change the grid's error. Keep its cells fixed and shrink only the step. The smearing grows from twelve to eighteen, then twenty-one, closing in on twenty-four. The exact pulse doesn't smear at all, so all of that is made by the method.
Suppose the picture hardly changes. Does that show it describes the real fluid?

No. Not by itself. Perhaps we've become very good at solving the wrong problem. If the cylinder is in the wrong place, or the outlet interferes with the wake behind it, more cells alone don't settle those questions.
And our flat world is a choice. Improving a two-dimensional calculation doesn't restore the third direction we left out. That is a question about the model, not just the mesh.
Rounding is another question. More digits can help when rounding matters. They won't put a misplaced cylinder back where it belongs. The remedy has to match the mistake.

We can also check balances, starting with the rate at which fluid crosses a face, which is called its flux. Does each shared face carry the same flux for its two neighbors? Does the pressure correction leave the declared divergence? Does the dye budget account for what enters and leaves?

Energy needs its own accounting. In a closed box with still walls and no applied forces, energy cannot rise. But a drop alone is not enough: compare it with the loss our declared viscosity predicts. In the wind tunnel, energy can enter through the boundary, so account for that too.

For tests with a known answer, measure the error directly. For the wake, compare a defined quantity, such as the time it takes to swing from side to side and back, under controlled changes. Agreeing with another calculation helps only if both calculations describe the same problem.

As in chapter twelve, we declare before we compare how small a change would matter for our question. Report what remains uncertain. We're building reasons to trust an answer, not waiting for every last pixel to stop moving.

Now we can spend our computation more intelligently. If some places need much smaller cells than others, can we put the detail there, and still keep every cell's ledger balanced where big cells meet small ones?

Back to our question card. Halving every cell takes four times as many cells, and under chapter twelve's neighbor rule, smaller cells need smaller steps too. But if the flow barely changes from one cell to the next somewhere, small cells there buy almost nothing.

So a program can split cells only where the flow needs more detail, and merge them back where it doesn't, as the flow changes. That's called an adaptive grid. It's a different idea from multigrid, whose coarse grids lived only inside the pressure solve.
How does it decide where? The wake is full of spinning air, so a natural first rule is to split cells wherever the air spins. Here's a flow where that rule fails.

This is an ideal flow past a cylinder, with no friction at all. The air parts in front, speeds up to twice the stream's speed at the sides, and closes again behind. We can write it down exactly, and nowhere in it does the air spin. As in chapter two, curving paths don't mean spinning air.

Now line up coarse cells along the line straight into the cylinder's front, each two radii wide. A coarse cell knows the speed at its two ends, and in between it can only draw a straight line. To test it, we check the true speed in the middle.
Spin is zero in every one of these cells. So is a coarse cell equally good everywhere along this line?

No. Three cells out, the straight line misses the middle by about two thousandths. Next to the cylinder, the air slows from almost full speed to a dead stop at the front, and the straight line misses by about three tenths. That's more than a hundred times worse.

So split a cell where its miss is bigger than a tolerance we choose, say one hundredth. Two cells qualify, the two nearest the cylinder. The row goes from six cells to eight, where halving everything would take twelve. A rule based on spin alone would split none of them.
Then the test runs again on the new cells. The two nearest the wall still miss by more than a hundredth, so they split again. A code repeats this down to the smallest cell size it allows.

So what's going on near the front, if not spin? The air is braking and turning aside, a squeezing and stretching called strain. But a straight line can follow a strain that's the same everywhere, perfectly. What it can't follow is a slope that keeps changing, and on this line, the slope changes fastest next to the cylinder.

Real flows add more, like the thin layer near a wall where the speed climbs from zero. The wall's own shape has to be drawn with cells. And the answer we want, the force on the cylinder, comes from pressure and friction all the way around its surface. Spin can be a useful clue, but on its own it doesn't measure error.

Real codes test something closer to what we just did. Basilisk, the free code from chapter ten, predicts each small cell's values from the coarser level, and splits where the prediction misses by more than a tolerance. Where the miss is well below it, cells merge back. In its own cylinder example, it tests the solid's outline, both parts of the velocity, and the dye.
But every split leaves a seam, where one big cell meets small ones. That's where the next problem lives.
Here's a seam. On the left, one big cell. On the right, two small cells, each half as tall. The big cell's right face is the small cells' two left faces, side by side.
Air flows across. Through the lower small face, one and a half units each step. Through the upper one, a half. So the small cells receive two units in all.
But suppose the big cell works out the flow across its own face from its coarser view, and gets two and a half. It loses two and a half, while the small cells gain two. Where does the extra half go?

Nowhere. It's simply lost, half a unit every step. In chapter seven, every inside face cancelled, because what left one cell entered the next. At a seam, that only works if the big face's flow equals the small faces' total.

Here are two cures. One builds the big face from the small ones, whose average speed is one, across a face two long, so exactly two. The other lets each side compute, then pays the difference back to the big cell afterward, which is called refluxing.

The second rule is for cells, when they merge or split. Say four small cells have dye levels of one, three, two and six. Merged, the big cell takes their average, three, and with four times the area, that's twelve units, as before. Copying one child's six instead would give twenty-four, and we'd have made dye.
Splitting runs the other way. The children may differ, to follow a slope, but what one gains, another must give up. So they still add back to the parent.

The third rule is balance. Split the big cell from our seam into four, and its outside faces keep their flows. But the new inside faces need values. A simple straight-line guess leaves two children out of balance, one losing half a unit each step, and one gaining half.
That's chapter nine's pressure puzzle again, on just these four cells. Solve it, let the pressure push on the inside faces, and all four children balance.

But that only works because the outside faces add up. Suppose the seam had disagreed, with the big cell's edge saying two and a half leave instead of two. Then the four imbalances would add up to a half, not zero. And no change inside could fix it, for the reason we saw in chapter seven.

So here's how these ideas sort out. Seams and transfers keep amounts, and balance keeps every cell's flow in and out equal. The wall's shape is its own problem, coming in chapter seventeen. And multigrid's coarse grids stay inside the pressure solve, while an adaptive grid changes the cells the flow itself lives on.

If any of these slips, a change of grid can give the flow a small kick, a pulse that comes from the grid, not the air. So a careful run checks the imbalance, and the force on the cylinder, just before and just after every change of grid.
Now the honest question. Did the adaptive grid save anything? Our row went to ten cells instead of twenty-four. But fewer cells isn't the same as less work.

Here's one hidden cost. In some codes, Basilisk among them, every cell takes the same time step. The cell that the air crosses in the shortest time sets that step for all of them. So one small cell with fast air in it can force short steps on the whole grid.

Suppose all three runs simulate the same flow for the same stretch of time. Each uses the shared step we just saw, and the air's speed sets it. The adaptive run's smallest cells match the uniform fine run's, a quarter as wide as the coarse run's, and the fastest air passes through them. Which takes more time steps, the uniform fine run or the adaptive one?

Then they take the same number, four times as many as the coarse run, because each step is a quarter as long. The adaptive run saves cells in each step, not steps. If viscosity sets the limit instead, through an explicit step as in chapter thirteen, the limit shrinks with the square of the cell width. Then both runs can need sixteen times as many.

Other costs hide too. The pressure puzzle still covers the whole tunnel every step, now with seams of its own. Deciding where to split, and moving values between grids, takes time. And keeping track of which cells are where takes memory.

So the comparison has to be fair. Three runs, uniform coarse, uniform fine and adaptive, on the same computer, with the same physics, the same walls and the same solver tolerance. And before running, we declare what we're measuring, and how close counts as close enough.

Here are two tables, the top one measured on a shear flow with no walls, the cylinder's all question marks until its runs are made. First the error in the measured answer, then cells, fluid and total, and time steps. Then time on the clock, memory, and the pressure puzzle's share. And last, the imbalance kick at each change of grid.

One trap is the box. The standard test for this flow, published in nineteen ninety-six so programs could be compared, is a channel more than five times as long as it is tall. Basilisk's adaptive grids start from a square, so about four fifths of that square lies outside the channel. The adaptive run must not take credit for skipping that space, so the fair baseline is a uniform grid covering just the channel.

In the measured shear flow, the fine and adaptive runs both passed the half-percent target. The adaptive run made sixty-four point eight percent fewer fluid-cell updates, and on this computer it took half a second. The fine run took one point zero five to one point zero seven seconds. Asking the pressure solver for a hundred times smaller imbalance left the adaptive error the same in every digit we show, and rounding wasn't tested. But a box with no walls and no wake says nothing yet about the cylinder. And if the adaptive run saves nothing there, or costs more, the table will say so, and so will we.
One part of all this depends on something we've drawn loosely so far, the shape of the cylinder itself. That's next.

Back to the cylinder's outline. Put the circle's center where four square cells meet, and call each cell solid or fluid, depending on whether its middle lies inside the circle. That simplest drawing turns the circle into a staircase.
Halve the cells, and the steps shrink. Every point of the staircase stays within about seven tenths of a cell width of the true circle, so halving the cells halves that limit.
But one thing doesn't improve. Walk around the circle, and the trip is about three point one four diameters. What happens to the trip around the staircase as the cells shrink?

It stays at exactly four diameters, at every size. Slide each step outward, and the pieces line up into a square around the circle. That's about a quarter too long, and every piece faces straight up, down, left or right, while the real wall turns smoothly through every direction.

Does that matter? The nineteen ninety-six comparison from chapter sixteen concluded that, for drag and lift, crude curved walls aren't accurate enough, even on very fine grids. Its most accurate solutions used grids shaped to fit the wall. On a square grid, one fix is to tell each cell how much of it is fluid, and where the real wall crosses it.

Now a worse mistake, one that refining can't see. Suppose the diameter we typed in is five percent too small. Each halving hugs that wrong circle more closely, and if the method converges, the answers settle down onto the answer for the wrong cylinder.

So it pays to solve a problem that's pinned down exactly, like the standard test from chapter sixteen. Its channel is two point two meters long and forty-one centimeters tall. Its cylinder is ten centimeters across, with fifteen centimeters of gap below it and sixteen above. Even that one centimeter of difference is part of the test.

At the walls and on the cylinder, the fluid doesn't slip, as in chapter six. At the inlet it arrives in a curved profile, still at the walls and fastest in the middle, at one and a half meters per second. On average, that's one meter per second.

The fluid isn't air, and with its viscosity, one number, average speed times diameter divided by viscosity, comes out at exactly one hundred. That's the Reynolds number, and the larger it is, the weaker viscosity's smoothing is, compared with the flow carrying itself along. In our equations, the same shape, boundaries and start, at the same Reynolds number, give the same pattern, just scaled in size and speed. And slow air follows those equations closely.
At the outlet, the test lets each group choose its own rule. As we said in chapter six, that rule is a choice, not nature's, so it goes in the ledger with everything else.

Every group reported the same few numbers. Two are peak forces, along the flow and across it, called drag and lift coefficients. One is how often the wake swings, the Strouhal number. And one is a pressure difference across the cylinder.

Here's one group's Strouhal number from the nineteen ninety-six report, on three grids, each with four times the unknowns of the last. Near point two nine seven, then just under point three, then just over it. The changes shrink, from about two and a half thousandths to under one thousandth. And the finer the time steps, the higher it came out.

That's convergence, the answer settling down as we refine. Measurements were made for this test too, and the Strouhal number came out at zero point two eight seven, give or take three thousandths. But the experiment's channel ran longer before the cylinder than the computed one did. What would close the gap?

Give the flow a longer run before the cylinder. With the inlet moved farther upstream, a computation in the same report gave zero point two eight nine, inside the measured range. The authors explain that, with the inlet so close, the flow arriving at the cylinder is slightly different.

So there are three different checks. Convergence asks whether the answer stops changing as we refine, and it tests how well we solved our equations. Benchmarking, agreeing with careful calculations of the very same problem, catches mistakes in our setup and our program, but it can't test the equations themselves. Validation asks whether it matches a measurement of the real setup, and only that tests whether our equations, shape and boundaries describe the real flow.
A cylinder is a long way from a car. So why not put a car shape in our tunnel and read off its drag?
Remember that our world is flat, and nothing in it changes in the direction we left out. So what does a flat car really stand for?
A car-shaped wall that never ends. Air can only go over it or under it, never around its sides. Around a real car, air does all three.
Underneath, a real car rolls along a road. Seen from the car, the road slides backward at the car's own speed, and the wheels turn. A flat picture has to make choices about both.

Then there's the spin. In three dimensions, a swirl can be stretched along its own axis, making it thinner and spinning it faster. In our flat world there's no direction to stretch it along. So without viscosity, or an added force that twists it, each parcel just keeps its spin as it's carried.

So a flat answer isn't simply a slice of a real one. A slice through a real flow can have air crossing it and changing along it, which the flat equations rule out. Even the nineteen ninety-six organizers found their changing three-dimensional tests harder than expected. For two of them, they couldn't settle reliable answers, and they left the test open.

And the numbers change scale. Our test runs at a Reynolds number of one hundred. A real car, four and a half meters long, at thirty meters per second in air, is near nine million. That's about ninety thousand times the Reynolds number in our test.
So if a car shape appears in our tunnel, it comes only after the cylinder passes its test, and it's labeled as a flat illustration. We won't read a real car's drag or downforce from it.
There's a quite different way to build a fluid simulator, called lattice Boltzmann. Instead of velocity and pressure, each cell keeps nine numbers.

Each one says how much fluid in the cell is moving one way, standing still, toward a side, or toward a corner. Every step, each moving amount hops exactly one cell in its own direction. Then, inside each cell, the nine amounts relax toward a balanced mix.
Add up a cell's nine amounts, and you get its density. Weight each by its direction, and you get its momentum. So this method reaches the same kind of flow, through different numbers.

How quickly the amounts relax sets the viscosity. We checked this with a small lattice Boltzmann program, separate from the solver this film builds. A decaying pattern of swirls ran on a grid of one hundred twenty-eight cells each way. It faded at the predicted rate, to within six thousandths of a percent.

Here's the catch. There's no pressure puzzle. Pressure is simply a third of the density, in the lattice's units, so pressure differences come from squeezing the fluid a little. And the same flow pattern, run faster, comes with bigger pressure differences.
So which flows will lattice Boltzmann handle most like our unsqueezable fluid, slow ones or fast ones?

Slow ones. For the same flow pattern, the squeeze grows with the square of the speed, measured against the lattice's own speed of sound. So the slower the flow, the less it squeezes, but wherever the pressure differs, as it does around our cylinder, it never becomes exactly unsqueezable.

Our method works the other way round. Its model fluid can't be squeezed at all. Each step, the pressure puzzle removes the squeeze, down to the leftover imbalance we met in chapter ten. These are two approximations of the same slow flow, wrong in different ways, and both must pass the same tests.

One more ingredient appears in some programs. When the grid is too coarse for the smallest swirls, they add extra viscosity where the flow shears hardest, to stand in for what's missing. That's a model, an extra assumption on top of the Navier-Stokes equations. It guesses the missing swirls' average effect, but it doesn't bring back their detail.
So a striking flat animation of a car, built this way, is an illustration. It can be honest and beautiful, and still not be a measurement of a real car.
Back to the tunnel, and the question we started with. Does halving the cells change the answer? To make our answer checkable, we give our tunnel the standard test's exact shape.

Here's the plan. Run the same flow on three grids, each with cells half as wide as the last, all at our smallest time step. Then run the finest grid again at two longer steps. Measure the swing rate, the forces through a whole swing as well as their peaks, and the pressure difference, every time, the same way.

And before running, we write down what counts as close enough. Then every entry stays a question mark until our runs fill it, including chapter sixteen's table, adaptive cells against uniform ones. Whatever those runs show, savings or none, goes in.

Here's where the answers should land. Another program's careful calculations of this same test, on the finest grid they report, put the drag coefficient's peak at about three point two three. The lift's peak is about zero point nine eight seven, just under one. And the Strouhal number is about zero point three zero two.

Even those are estimates. In nineteen ninety-six, the organizers' estimated range for the lift peak ran from zero point nine nine to one point zero one. Later reference calculations put it just below that range.

Here's a prediction you can check. A Strouhal number of about zero point three, an average speed of one meter per second, and a cylinder a tenth of a meter across. How many full swings should the wake make each second?

About three. Strouhal number times speed, divided by size, gives about three point oh two swings per second, one every third of a second. That's a number any run of this test can be checked against, by counting its swings against a clock.
One honest label for the picture itself. The dye we release at the inlet is a record of the past, as in chapter two. A curl in the dye still isn't proof of a swirl in the flow.

So which swirls belong to the flow, and which did our computer invent, or erase? Now we know how to ask. Halve the cells and the steps, check the walls, the inlet and the outlet, compare with careful published answers to the same test, and write it all down.
